paragraphs.text: A [tuo](sheng:pressing) of [raw pu’er](sheng:identity) pressed at the Menghai factory in 1998 and graded Jia Ji, Grade A, for leaf above the factory’s standard production. Menghai was one of the [state factories](sheng:history) that made pu’er to set recipes after 1949. The tuo is a small bowl shape, first pressed so tea packed well for the old trade routes, and a small piece like this ages faster than a large, tight cake.

The shop’s notes record it as aged in warm storage. Heat and humidity decide how fast raw pu’er changes, so a [warm store](sheng:storage) moves it along quickly. The trade does not agree where [aged raw pu’er](sheng:ageing) begins: some count from ten years, many wait for twenty or more. This tuo is past both marks, and the notes place it between young sheng and fully aged.

brewing.text: Pry the leaf off a cake or brick in chunks with a pick or knife, from the surface and toward the centre, rather than crumbling it. A mix of larger pieces and smaller ones brews evenly. Young raw pu’er takes water a little off the boil, about 85 to 95°C, because hotter water draws out more of its bitterness; an aged one takes 95°C to boiling. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and a quick rinse of a few seconds, then a first steep of ten to fifteen seconds, adding a few seconds each round. A good raw tea gives eight to ten cups or more.

notice.text: A smoother, thicker, sweeter cup with woody, herbal and camphor notes and something of dried dates or dark fruit.
